rows.title: Managerial Accounting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Perform cost-volume-profit analysis and prepare various budgets to provide management with relevant information in planning activities.
Use variance analysis and performance measurement methods to provide feedback about product, segment, management, and company performance.
Apply cost information using various allocation and accumulation methods.
Analyze relevant information for management decision-making.

rows.title: Ethics and Moral Reasoning in Criminal Justice
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify ethical issues that often arise for criminal justice professionals.
Analyze theories of moral development and leadership and their influence on ethical problem solving.
Compare common theories of ethical decision making and methods to reinforce procedural practices and social justice in a diverse society.
Apply ethical principles and standards of justice to cases involving police corruption, abuse of power, and judicial/attorney misconduct.

rows.title: Concepts of Criminal Law
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interpret the concept of corpus delicti and how it informs the prosecution of general crimes, crimes against people, and property crimes.
Discuss the principles of constitutional law (Bill of Rights), and how the three branches of government administer those guidelines.
Utilize the California Penal Code to interpret basic criminal law terminology.
Explore arrest, search, and seizure principles, and the effect statutory and case law has on law enforcement practices.

rows.title: Principles and Procedures of the Justice System
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and describe the stages in the trial process
Identify and critically analyze the concepts of due process as found in the 6th, 8th, and 14th amendments, including right to counsel, bail, and jury trial
Describe the history and application of the exclusionary rule in shaping criminal procedure
Describe application of the right to counsel in a criminal case
Describe application of the right to a jury trial

rows.title: Introduction to Administration of Justice
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain traditional and contemporary theories of crime and criminal behavior.
Distinguish the levels of criminal offense and the possible pathways of a criminal suspect through the criminal justice system.
Explain the structure and functions of the California and federal court systems and the factors that affect sentencing in those systems.
Identify and critique modern problems in the criminal justice system.

rows.title: Criminal Investigation
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Execute appropriate preliminary investigation related to crime scene examination.
Analyze various investigative techniques for specific criminal offenses.
Distinguish critical ethical issues.
Analyze the investigator's role that leads to criminal court proceedings and the trial process.

rows.title: Progressive Policing in the 21st Century
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the history of community policing in the contexts of race and class.
Explain the intersection of police, leadership, and community organizational models in the traditional and progressive policing eras.
Examine how both crime and fear inform progressive policing.
Describe the evolution of progressive policing techniques, their implementation, and efficacy.

rows.title: Forensic Evidence
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the history of forensic science, the structure and organization of crime labs, and the sub-disciplines of forensic science.
Explain the roles of forensic and investigative personnel and articulate a realistic perspective of the field of forensic science.
Select the appropriate methods of analysis used for biological, chemical, physical fit, and pattern evidence.
Evaluate the criteria for admission of scientific evidence in court and expert testimony, and the types and sources of error in forensic science.

rows.title: Criminal Justice Report Writing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Gather complete and relevant information from victims, suspects, and witnesses for useful field notes.
Write organized reports that are clear and mechanically correct.
Use the professional codes and conventions of criminal justice communications.

rows.title: Patrol Procedures
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the basic functions and purpose of police patrol.
Describe police procedures and codes of conduct.
Demonstrate required skills for San Francisco City College Campus Police Department patrol.
Describe the knowledge and physical skills necessary in preparing for the San Francisco Police Department entrance examination.

rows.title: Police Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Execute the practical and typical duties of a Police Officer as assigned while working under direct or indirect supervision.
Apply the theory, techniques, and knowledge gained in the law enforcement curriculum in a positive manner.
Utilize radio communications and police equipment in a proper and safe manner.
Exhibit professional behavior as it relates to the law enforcement code of ethics.

rows.title: Criminal Justice Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Utilize a glossary of terms and definitions unique to the assigned agency
Describe the functions and services provided by the assigned agency in order to complete assigned tasks
Illustrate professional attitudes while working with the public and members at the internship site
Display promptness, responsibility and courtesy in the work experience agency
Compare the theoretical and practical functions of the criminal justice system relative to the agency assigned

rows.title: P.C. 832 Arrest and Control Certification
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the perspective of a law enforcement officer to distinguish professionalism, ethics, and the components of a community policing program.

Analyze the differences between the powers of arrest of a private person and a peace officer, evaluating the laws of evidence and their relationship to U.S. Constitutional Amendments and the criminal justice system.
Produce a written police report containing the proper information from a crime scene.
Apply proper handcuffing, search, arrest, and control techniques, following POST standards and keeping within the guidelines of force relative to reasonable and lethal force.

rows.title: The Black Experience in California
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the scholarly work of African Americans to explain the historical and political reasons Africans were brought to the "New World" during the Early Colonial Era and the ensuing social struggles and lived experiences of African American communities.

Analyze how race and racism impacted the cultural realities and experiences of early African and African American people in California in areas such as class, gender, language, national origin, religion, sexuality, sovereignty, and spirituality.
Utilize historical sources to analyze how the intersectionality of race and racism has shaped survival techniques and cultural identity of African Americans in California.
Analyze effective interpersonal and inter-ethnic group interactions for African people to successfully gain agency and thrive in the American West and the U.S.

rows.title: From Funk to Hip Hop
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the social condition of Black people expressed in various syntheses, adaptations, and genres of Black popular music.
Explain the social and cultural links and messages of solidarity and resistance for racial justice between Black music before and since the birth of the hip-hop era of the 1980s.
Analyze how popular Black musicians impacted liberation movements by calling out systemic racism and racial injustice.
Evaluate the importance of culturally expressive styles and the socio-political implications of Black popular music on U.S. race relations.
Assess the rich historical connections between musical migrations, cultural interchanges, and the intersectionality of race and gender that gave rise to hip hop.

rows.title: American Sign Language Part I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and use American Sign Language with elementary linguistic structures appropriate to a variety of language functions.
Explain general historical factors and contexts that have contributed to American Deaf culture and the development of American Sign Language.
Examine culturally appropriate behavior with Deaf people in various social situations.

rows.title: Biological Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the biological and environmental factors responsible for modern human variation.
Define the scope, focus, and subdisciplines of biological anthropology.
Analyze simple problems in human genetics.
Compare the morphology, evolution, classification, and behavior of non-human primates.
Evaluate the fossil evidence for hominin evolution using the methods and theories of archaeology and paleoanthropology.

rows.title: Indigenous Peoples of North America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the relationship of North American indigenous cultures and the natural environment using the anthropological culture area approach.
Compare different traditional North American indigenous cultures in a nonethnocentric manner using anthropological concepts.
Analyze and contrast anthropological and non-anthropological sources of information about indigenous North American cultures.
Analyze precontact and postcontact North American indigenous cultures using an anthropological perspective.
Compare traditional North American indigenous cultures with present day North American indigenous cultures.
Analyze challenges faced by Native American indigenous peoples today in relationship to sociopolitical and economic issues.

rows.title: Biological Anthropology Laboratory
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the scientific method to basic research questions in biological anthropology.
Apply knowledge of human genetics to problem solving in Mendelian, non-Mendelian, and population genetics.
Perform and record scientific measurements of human variation.
Describe, measure, and analyze contemporary and fossil human and non-human primate skeletal material.
Observe and record characteristics of primate behavior.

rows.title: Queer Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and apply key terminology and methods in the study of queer anthropology.
Compare key theoretical frameworks that influence the perceptions and experiences of queer individuals around the world.
Analyze the major institutions, cultural forces, and practices that determine queer status.
Assess how anthropology contributes to our understanding of global conceptions of queer cultures.

rows.title: Introduction to Social and Cultural Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and analyze cross-cultural variations in the diverse ways of life around the world
Compare the field of cultural anthropology to the other sub-fields of anthropology
Apply the methods of anthropological research and cultural description while applying ethics-based principles
Analyze the major theoretical perspectives and concepts of cultural anthropology

rows.title: Introduction to Linguistic Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the nature and structure of human language, and compare its acquisition process to various forms of non-verbal communication.
Use the methods of phonological analysis to assess individual languages.
Describe the biological foundations of language, and the relationships between language and thought.
Examine the influence of language on values, behavior, and inter- and intra-cultural exchanges.
Describe linguistic change and the lexical reconstruction method used to infer time span, movements, and overall cultural content of population groups.

rows.title: Magic, Witchcraft, and Religion
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the anthropology of religion and its primary concerns.
Analyze and evaluate the theories and contributions of major researchers in the anthropology of magic, witchcraft, and religion.
Utilize participant observation of a religious, spiritual, or supernatural ritual or event as an ethnographic method of anthropological research.
Interpret and describe differing religious and magical belief systems in a relativistic and holistic manner using ethnographic and/or historical examples.

rows.title: Architecture Design Studio I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create architectonic solutions to a set of abstract problems
Evaluate a proposed architectonic solution against the problem requirements
Analyze and communicate designs and design precedents visually, orally, and in physical model using an architectural vocabulary
Apply a visual language that is two- and three-dimensional responsive to form, space, and context
Examine how architects and interior designers create sets of functional and sustainable solutions

rows.title: Architecture Design Studio III
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create architectural solutions to a set of project requirements
Produce documents analyzing various aspects of the urban environment
Analyze the impact of programmatic requirements and site parameters in the design process
Communicate the design process visually, orally, in writing, and by models (physical and digital)

rows.title: Fundamentals of Building Structures
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Consider the major constraints and impacts related to the selection of structural systems
Explain how structural systems respond to loads, including natural forces
Assess the performance of materials in a structural system

rows.title: Architectural Graphics I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze systems used in architectural design drawings.
Create orthographic, paraline and perspective drawings that communicate simple architectural design intentions.
Use both analog and digital drawing tools and understand their affect and potential for graphic communication.
Interpret the correct use of architectural scale, drawing symbols, line weights, and line types that follow architectural graphic conventions.

rows.title: Fundamentals of Rhino 3D
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Navigate the software's interface, work flow, and NURBS geometry.
Create three-dimensional digital models using 3D basic modeling tools, poly-surfaces and modeling aids to represent a designed object.
Modify, edit, analyze, and transform existing digital three-dimensional surface models, using algorithms to create and edit 3D geometry.
Construct a prototype, document with annotation, and render a digital three-dimensional surface model.

rows.title: Fundamentals of the International Building Code
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the history and purpose of model building codes including how they are developed, managed, kept up to date, and enforced.
Analyze how provisions of the IBC can apply to the design and planning of various building types.
Apply appropriate research methods to conduct building code research relevant to architectural projects.

rows.title: Freehand Drawing II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply freehand drawing skills (without the use of straight edge tools) to create sketches of the existing or proposed built environment using correct proportions.
Recall the key components of linear perspective and analyze their principles in communicating form in the built environment.
Employ one-point, two-point and three-point linear perspective techniques in freehand drawing to analyze architectural form, structure and context.
Use varied monochromatic and polychromatic drawing media to depict form, value and texture in freehand drawing.

rows.title: History of Architecture II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare significant features, characteristics and representative buildings of various architectural movements since 1400 C.E. using accurate terminology and interpreted through visual environmental literacy.
Evaluate how cultural, climatic, ecological, technological, socioeconomic, and public health conditions have impacted the design of the built environment since 1400 C.E.
Analyze the ways architecture has served diverse human needs, values, and aspirations since 1400 C.E.

rows.title: Ancient Art and Architecture of Latin America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the different art styles of the major cultures of ancient Latin America.
Compare selected ancient Latin American cultures and their beliefs.
Analyze how Latin American ancient art styles reflect their cultural context.
Analyze how geographical locations and conditions are reflected in the beliefs, styles, and customs of each culture.

rows.title: African-American Art History
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ historical and visual literacy methods in order to analyze African and African American art and architecture.
Compare and distinguish styles, trends, periods and art movements in African and African-American art
Evaluate works of art with regard to their social, political, and cultural contexts.
Discuss works of art by pivotal African and African-American artists.
Analyze African American and Afro-centered thematic, content and formal stylistic elements created by Africans and African-Americans.

rows.title: History of Contemporary Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the variety of techniques and formal visual elements of individual works of art in different media.
Define the various styles of late modern and contemporary art to analyze their components and characteristics.
Evaluate the historical factors which led to the emergence, development and subsequent history of late modern and contemporary art movements/styles.
Examine and assess works of art in relation to the historical, cultural, and sociological context in which they were created.
Compare stylistic elements that distinguish aesthetic and cultural trends of pivotal works of art by major artists in late modern and contemporary art.

rows.title: Arts of Africa, Oceania, and Indigenous North America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and analyze the formal visual elements and techniques of individual works of art in different media.
Compare the stylistic aspects and trends in the art of Africa, Oceania, and Indigenous North America.
Evaluate and differentiate works of art in relation to the historical and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Analyze the historical roles and functions of art, architecture, and the artist.

rows.title: 18th-Century French Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and differentiate 18th-century works of French art with reference to formal elements and style.
Identify connections between 18th-century French art and ideas.
Analyze the social functions of art in 18th-century France.
Evaluate the historical significance of 18th-century French art.

rows.title: 19th-Century Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and differentiate 19th-century paintings with reference to formal elements and style.
Identify connections between 19th-century art and ideas.
Analyze the social functions of art in the 19th century.
Evaluate the historical significance of individual works of 19th-century art.

rows.title: Advanced Design: 3D Foundations
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create three-dimensional forms that demonstrate basic knowledge and understanding of elements and organizing principles of design.
Employ innovative problem solving through the use of materials and development of form when designing for a specific problem.
Apply careful and thoughtful elementary visual analysis of three-dimensional form through writing and verbal discussion.
Identify the use of design principles and elements in the creation of design and art objects in various cultures throughout history.

rows.title: Basic Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply beginning-level drawing techniques effectively using a range of materials.
Utilize drawing concepts to effectively and creatively solve problems at the beginning level.
Analyze drawings from diverse cultures with regard to formal qualities and social and historical aspects.
Evaluate one’s own beginning-level drawings and the work of peers in terms of formal qualities and communicative aspects.

rows.title: Beginning Figure Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply beginning-level drawing techniques and media to accurately draw proportional human figures from life.
Apply a beginning-level understanding of major muscle groups and bone structures to figure drawing.
Analyze figure drawings across diverse cultural contexts, exploring beginning-level formal qualities and social-historical significance.
Analyze one's own work and the work of peers using beginning-level critical thinking skills and vocabulary.

rows.title: Introduction to Illustration
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify principal areas in the field of illustration, considering foundational cultural, historical contexts and contemporary issues.
Solve illustrative problems effectively and creatively at a beginning level.
Apply beginning-level dry and wet material techniques in support of content.
Analyze illustration work using beginning-level design principles and illustration vocabulary to evaluate content and artistic expression.

rows.title: Beginning Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ materials and techniques fundamental to the construction of paintings in several styles and genres.
Organize elements of design and color into effective painted compositions.
Apply the skills necessary to develop ideas into personally-expressive paintings.
Analyze historical and contemporary styles of painting and discuss their relevance to painting now.

rows.title: Beginning Watercolor Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the variety of watercolor pigments and painting processes.
Apply brushwork skills with paint effectively on paper.
Create textures using varying methods and additive mediums.
Solve basic painting errors using correcting techniques.
Apply vocabulary of watercolor when critiquing paintings.
Mix colors using basic color theory as a guide.

rows.title: Intermediate Chinese Brush Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply intermediate-level techniques in classical and contemporary Chinese calligraphy and painting using traditional materials.
Analyze the poetic, philosophical, and symbolic content in historical and contemporary Chinese brush paintings to inform expressive personal work.
Utilize traditional Chinese aesthetic principles—such as the use of color, line, shape, layering, and tonal variation—to solve visual problems at the intermediate level.
Evaluate student's own brush paintings and those of peers in terms of formal qualities, technical execution, cultural content, and expressive intent.

rows.title: Intermediate Intaglio and Relief Printmaking
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze contemporary and historical prints of diverse cultures.
Use intermediate intaglio and relief plate making techniques to create print editions that exhibit a development of imagery and technique.
Use intermediate intaglio and relief printing techniques to create print editions that exhibit a development of imagery and technique.
Analyze, evaluate, and revise work based on proofing and critiques.
Practice safe working methods when using equipment, tools, and supplies.

rows.title: Intermediate Ceramics
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply new skills and techniques to create artwork at the intermediate level.
Integrate three-dimensional design principles as they apply to structure and aesthetics in artwork at an intermediate level.
Evaluate artwork in a critical thinking process that supports individual creative expression at an intermediate level.
Research contemporary and historical ceramics that relate to the students’ personal artwork.

rows.title: Intermediate Sculpture
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Practice safe working methods when using sculpture tools and materials.
Evaluate technical aspects, composition, craft, material choice, and content when discussing sculptural forms.
Produce artwork that demonstrates intermediate understanding of additive and subtractive sculptural processes using applicable tools and materials.

rows.title: Survey of Art from Prehistory to the Medieval Era
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from prehistory to the medieval era employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from prehistory to the medieval era.

rows.title: Introduction to Asian American Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and investigate critical ethnic studies concepts including race, ethnicity, equity, anticolonization, eurocentrism, Orientalism, and settler colonialism, and other racially constructed power structures as conceptual contexts for studying Asian American histories and current issues.
Identify and analyze relevant U.S. governmental actions, law, and policies, and their impacts on Asian Americans past and present.

Analyze with relevant theory produced by and about Asian American communities the intersectionality of Asian American lived experiences along various vectors of identity, including race and ethnicity, gender and sexuality, socioeconomic class and labor, national origin, mixed heritages, religion/spirituality, generation, age, and ability.

Review critically how Asian American social justice and political activism, resistance to Eurocentric racialization, and solidarity, from early immigration to the present, are relevant to current and structural issues.

Engage actively with anti-racist, anti-colonial issues, theories, practices, and movements in Asian American communities, applying knowledge and service ethics towards diversity and equity in and out of the classroom.
Analyze the term "Asian American" as a category constructed in response to legal and social exclusion.

rows.title: Asian American Experience Since 1820
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the impact of racialized and ethnocentric United States government policies on Asian immigrants and Asian American participation in civic duties and social justice movements.
Apply Asian American produced theories and methodologies of social and behavioral science inquiry in Asian American Studies.
Analyze intersectionality within the Asian American experience in the United States, as race and racism relate to age, class, gender, language, national origin, religion, and sexuality.

Summarize the diverse Asian immigration experience, including socio-cultural, economic and political conditions, critical events, histories and traditions, that have impacted Asian American communities’ efforts to gain agency and build an equitable and just society.

Review critically how Asian American struggles and resistance for racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by diverse communities, are relevant to current and structural issues

rows.title: Asian Americans and American Ideals and Institutions
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Review critically how Asian Pacific Americans gained growing citizenship rights and obligations, including applying concepts and theories of race and equity.
Analyze how Asian Pacific Americans have exercised their rights and responsibilities as citizens, at local, state, and national levels, including histories of oppression and agency.

Compare how different nationalities of Asian Pacific Americans have historically been treated by the political process and institutions under the U.S. Constitution and California Constitution, including Ethnic Studies and Critical Race frameworks developed to interpret these experiences.
Evaluate how Asians in America have been affected by the political philosophies of the framers of the Constitution throughout United States history.

Analyze how Asian Pacific Americans have leveraged the relationships of local and California state government with the federal government, enacting struggle and solidarity to challenge structural issues.

rows.title: Asian American Issues Through Film
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and articulate how society influences the interpretation and message of films, specifically with regard to race and ethnicity, critically reviewing the intertextual relationships between Asian American historical archetypes in American cinema.

Analyze representations by both mainstream and independent media of the intersectionality of race and racism with class, gender, sexuality, religion, immigration status and other aspects of Asian American lived experiences and their impact on Asian Americans.

Assess the critical impacts of independent productions in Asian American media on American mainstream representations of Asian Americans, interpreting those portrayals in relation to struggle, social justice, current issues and national policies.

Evaluate the ways diasporic or transnational cinema from Asia influence representations of Asian Americans in American media, including applying Ethnic Studies theory and knowledge to describe the connection between film portrayals and critical events in the histories, cultures and intellectual traditions, with special focus on agency and group-affirmation.

Compare similar film content from different perspectives (outsider perspectives versus insider perspectives), applying theories and methodologies of social and behavioral science and Ethnic Studies in the exploration of Asian American films.

Formulate an analytical Ethnic Studies framework for uncovering, evaluating, and challenging stereotypes, bias, and misrepresentation in films, by articulating Ethnic Studies concepts such as race and racism, racialization, and anti-racism in analyzing film images of Asians.

rows.title: Chinese American Community
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the ways in which race and racism, ethno-centrism, white supremacy, struggle and resistance have influenced the experience of the Chinese American community over time.

Describe the Chinese contributions to the development of the multi-ethnic society in the United States and evaluate how these contributions have been a source of agency for the Chinese American community.
Evaluate the impacts of public policy on Chinese American communities, using Ethnic Studies theory and intersectional knowledge of race, class, and gender.
Apply theory and knowledge produced by Asian Americans to understand critical events, histories, lived experiences and social struggles in Chinese American communities.

rows.title: Stories of Asian America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate critically the intersection of race and racism with gender, class, sexuality, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, language, and/or age, as expressed in literature and lived experiences of Asian Americans.

Analyze the critical content and contexts of Asian American writings within the social, historical, intellectual traditions of lived-experiences, emphasizing agency and group-affirmation and applying knowledge and theory produced by Asian American authors.
Evaluate sources of tension and conflict within Asian American families and identity, as represented in literature, particularly along lines of gender and generation.

Assess the contributions Asian American creative expression has made to America, applying an aesthetic understanding of the ways in which Asian Americans have created fine and performing arts, linguistic expression, philosophical reasoning, and analytical or creative writing.

Analyze through literature the impact of migration on community formation and transnational connections, exploring communal, national, international, and transnational structural issues, Asian American resistance and struggles for racial and social justice.
Describe and actively engage with how Asian American authors and communities have approached anti-racist and anti-colonial issues, practices, and movements to build a more just and equitable society.

rows.title: Individual Study in Asian American Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Design measurable objectives to evaluate project progress.
Analyze aspects of the Asian American experience based on independent research.
Assess results of projects and make recommendations for further actions.

rows.title: East Asian Calligraphy: An Introduction
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Comprehend writing systems, scripts, and aesthetic principles of East Asian calligraphy in cultural/historical backgrounds.
Analyze the relationship between calligraphy and philosophy/religion/art in China, Japan, and Korea.
Practice the discipline, techniques, and training of East Asian calligraphy.

rows.title: Manga and Anime
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Classify the major historical events, individuals, and organizations in the development of manga and anime.

rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Utilize safe working practices in compliance with sanitation codes in a bulk production kitchen.
Evaluate cooking theory and techniques and their uses in bulk production.
Produce dishes in bulk using a variety of cooking techniques, bulk production equipment, and ingredients.
Identify and fabricate various cuts of proteins, including meats, poultry, and seafood for use in a bulk production kitchen.
Apply advanced kitchen mathematical concepts to bulk production.

rows.title: Meat Analysis
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the various cuts and grades of beef, pork, veal, and lamb.
Explain the classifications of fowl, including chicken, turkey, squab, and duck.
Describe the proper techniques in fabricating beef, pork, veal, and lamb.
Utilize a variety of techniques in cutting up poultry and fish.
Explore cooking methods that are suitable for various meats, poultry, and fish.

rows.title: Restaurant Operations: Front of House, Fine Dining
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ skills and behaviors that respect differences and contribute to guest satisfaction.
Summarize the evolution of service styles and trends in restaurant operations.
Apply costing principles and menu pricing methods to front-of-house operations.
Use common dining room equipment and tools to run operations efficiently.
Apply safety, sanitation, and personal hygiene principles to front-of-house operations.

rows.title: Hospitality Marketing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess key marketing concepts and principles in the hospitality industry.
Summarize consumer perspectives and measure key marketing methodologies in the hospitality industry.
Assess the impact of social media on hospitality businesses.
Apply reputation management skills.

rows.title: Fundamentals of Contemporary Hospitality Law
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and apply fundamental legal concepts and terminology integral to the hospitality industry.
Analyze and apply the rights and duties of a hospitality operator in relation to their guests and employees from diverse backgrounds, ethnicities, and classes.
Develop strategies to prevent and reduce liability through pro-active management, compliance and education techniques.

rows.title: Fundamentals of Hospitality Financial Reports
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply cash or accrual-basis accounting to prepare an Income Statement.
Use multiple analyses to interpret both restaurant and hotel rooms department operations.
Apply fixed and variable cost analysis to hospitality planning and decision making to help achieve profit objectives.
Summarize and distinguish between the major components of hotel and restaurant financial statements.

rows.title: Sustainability in the Hospitality Industry
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify key events and their impact on the development of sustainable thought and practices
List and explain the environmental, social, and economic challenges in the hospitality industry
Determine opportunities and goals to improve sustainable practices in the hospitality industry
Apply a systems approach to sustainability in relationship to hospitality, the culinary arts, and tourism
Construct coherent and sound arguments on sustainability issues in the hospitality industry.

rows.title: Classic & Modern Sauces
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the history, trends, and fundamentals of classic and modern saucemaking.
Compare classic and modern sauces techniques and methods of preparation.
Determine how sauces are paired with various foods.
Prepare a variety of classic, modern, and global sauces.

rows.title: Global Cuisines: Italy
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the influences on Italian cuisine including history, geography, and climate.
Define various terminology pertaining to Italian cuisine.
Explain and apply the various flavor profiles, ingredients, cooking techniques, and equipment used in Italian cuisine.
Compare the various similarities and differences between cuisines of various regions of Italy and the influence of Italian cuisine on other countries.
Use knives, tools, and equipment, both classic and modem, properly and safely.

rows.title: Advanced Pastry Doughs, Batters, and Creams
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Practice proper food safety and sanitation appropriate for a professional pastry shop.
Discuss the origins and processes of producing specialized pastry doughs, batters and related creams.
Compose creations of specialized pastry doughs, batters, and creams by demonstrations and topic-focused material.
Examine dietary restrictions in pastry doughs, batter, and cream.

rows.title: Mousses: Cakes and Desserts
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Practice proper food safety and sanitation appropriate for a professional pastry shop.
Use tools and equipment properly and safely in a professional pastry shop setting.
Employ techniques for production of a variety of mousse cakes and individual mousse-based desserts.

rows.title: Cooking for Vegetarian and Other Special Diets
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Differentiate between vegetarian, vegan, and various special diets.
Apply various cooking techniques necessary for special diets.
Use specialized techniques and equipment safely and properly to ensure that the food is wholesome and safe.
Create menus that take into account health and cultural dietary restrictions.

rows.title: Introduction to Violence Intervention
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain violence and trauma and how they have been conceptualized and treated over history.
Evaluate the role of intersectionality, culture, and history and how each shapes one's response to trauma exhibited by young children.
Describe the symptoms, behavioral patterns, and underlying psychological and biological changes in young children who are exposed to violence and trauma.
Identify intervention and prevention strategies found in early education environment and community organizations.

rows.title: Children's Healthy Eating & Nutrition
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Examine the relationship between child growth and development and nutritional needs and eating behaviors
Assess dietary adequacy using appropriate food guidance systems and current dietary guidelines to promote and maintain health.
Analyze the impact of food security and health disparities on families to increase access to nutritious and affordable food.
Apply basic food management and safe handling skills to plan and create simple and healthy meals and snacks.
Plan, conduct, and evaluate effective techniques and resources for providing age appropriate nutrition education to youth.

rows.title: Work Experience in Child Development
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Observe child development theory in practical application and identify how an environment and setting meets the developmental needs of children.
Demonstrate self-assessment skills and the ability to inventory workplace competencies.
Use ethical and professional behavior in the work setting.
Discuss, compare, and contrast work experience placement and role of child care and education in the community.
Assess suitability of child development and education for career options.

rows.title: Children with ADHD
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Categorize ADHD symptoms and behaviors, including hyperactive and inattentive symptoms.
Analyze the over- or under-diagnosis of ADHD.
Apply analysis of ADHD "symptoms" to define inclusive strategies to support children's learning.
Identify pros and cons of various treatment methods used to treat ADHD.

rows.title: Learning Disabilities
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze various specific learning disabilities including symptoms and warning signs.
Select inclusive strategies, including multisensory strategies, to support children with learning differences to promote their full success in the classroom.
Describe community resources to help with identification, assessment, and remediation of learning disabilities.

rows.title: Children's Emotional Development
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze origins of children's emotional and behavioral challenges.
Plan approaches to building young children's emotional competence and coping skills.
Identify skills for co-regulation and the role of self-awareness and self-reflection for adults.

rows.title: Issues in CDEV - Teacher Seminar
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze assessment, curriculum, equity and/or teaching skills related to the classroom or the field.
Explain how equity and inclusion are infused into program quality, assessments, curriculum or teaching.
Translate anti-bias and culturally sensitive theory into teaching practice.

rows.title: Starting A Large Family Child Care or Center
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply key principles of developmental needs and supportive practices for children in the context of child care programs and facilities.
Apply knowledge of laws, regulations and community resources for California licensed child care programs.
Select and use appropriate business strategies for successful child care programs.
Analyze staff training and educational requirements for child care program personnel.

rows.title: Communicating with Families in Family Child Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the goals of communication between providers and families for the well-being of children, families, and the family child care.
Interpret Title 22 Licensing Requirements for Family Child Care relating to parent-guardian communication and parents' rights.

Develop strategies for quality family-provider communication respecting children's development, being sensitive toward diverse childrearing values and practices, and using anti-bias communication skills.

rows.title: Advanced Business Practices in Family Child Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply developmentally appropriate practice, licensing, and inclusion requirements to policies and materials in family child care settings.
Design materials and policies for successful family child care businesses.

rows.title:
Infant/Toddler Curriculum in Family Child
Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the principles of early development in infants and toddlers.
Apply Developmentally Appropriate Practices (DAP) to meet the needs of infants and toddlers in order to support their optimal growth and development in a Family Child Care (FCC) setting.

rows.title: Music and Movement in Family Child Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the benefits of music and movement for young children in all areas of development.
Plan a program of music and movement activities that are developmentally and cultural appropriate for the children in the family child care.
Demonstrate strategies for structuring and guiding music and movement experiences for young children.
Identify resources in the community that support and enhance the music and movement experiences for young children.

rows.title: Mixed Ages in Family Child Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Differentiate the developmental needs of infants, toddlers, preschoolers and school-age children in family child care.
Plan environments, daily schedules and activities that address the needs, interest and safety of all age groups.
Explain strategies to maximize the social and cognitive benefits of having children of mixed ages together in family child care.
Evaluate one's own ability to care for all ages in a family child care setting.

rows.title: Early Autism Spectrum Disorders
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Define Autism Spectrum Disorders and the symptoms and common misunderstandings.
Examine current theories of intervention and controversies surrounding ASD assessment and diagnosis.
Compare ASD resources for families.

rows.title: ECE Teacher-Child Interactions Using the Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS)
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Define the components of the domains and dimensions of the Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS).
Integrate the Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS) dimensions for supportive interactions between teachers and young children in early childhood classroom practice.

rows.title: Infant/Toddler Growth and Development
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate ways in which a secure attachment relationship is the foundation for development in the first three years of a young child's life.
Evaluate roles of families and societal influences on the socialization of infants and toddlers.
Differentiate changes in physical/sensory-motor, social-emotional, and cognitive/language development through each stage of the first three years.
Analyze the effects and interactions of inborn traits and environmental influences on development in the first three years.
Use developmental theories and methodologies to analyze infant/toddler development.

rows.title: Introduction to Stress Reduction and Coping in Early Childhood and Elementary School Programs
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the theories and explain the origins and causes of stress.
Consider the importance of the teacher's role and responsibilities in creating a stress-free, inclusive learning environment that incorporates the uniqueness of each student.
Employ the referral process as a means of prevention and intervention using assessment tools that are developmentally and culturally appropriate.

Recognize and identify their students and self-behaviors that are an adaptive/maladaptive stress response and then use this information to create developmental and culturally appropriate prevention and intervention strategies.

rows.title: Introduction to Early Childhood Curriculum
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Investigate and apply developmentally appropriate principles and teaching strategies to positively influence all young children's development and acquisition of knowledge and skills.
Evaluate the caregiver's/teacher's role in providing best and promising practices in early childhood programs.
Compare play-based curriculum that supports children's cognitive, language, creative, physical, social and emotional development.

Design and implement curriculum based on observation and assessment to support play and learning using deveopmental, inclusive, and anti-bias principles in colloboration with families to support all children.

rows.title: Interactions with Children
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate childhood behavior.
Explain brain development and sensory integration in the preschool years.
Identify and evaluate different parenting and teaching styles.
Analyze the key indicators of quality environments for all children, including those with special needs.

rows.title: Supervised Field Experience in Early Childhood Education: Practicum
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Integrate understanding of children's development and needs to develop appropriate programs, curriculum and learning environments for all children.
Apply effective approaches to support positive relationships with children and adults.
Apply knowledge of the National Association for the Education of Young Children (NAEYC) Code of Ethical Conduct to professional practice within early childhood education settings.
Evaluate feedback from mentor teacher and apply it to professional development.

rows.title: Children with Special Needs
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the range of special needs common to children in early childhood.
Explain the impact of early intervention strategies.
Describe inclusion and develop an inclusive curriculum that includes intervention strategies.
Identify community resources available for early childhood educators as well as children with special needs and their families.

rows.title: Community Youth Work Support
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess the effectiveness of individual and group activities and teaching strategies appropriate to a youth-serving program.
Analyze the roles of adults, administrators, youth workers, supervisors, and leadership in youth-serving organizations.
Critique one's own work experiences to guide and inform practice.

rows.title: Relationship-based Infant/Toddler Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze how program policies support relationships in infant/toddler care.
Describe a child's behavior with an understanding of social-emotional development and possible underlying causes of that behavior.
Plan activities and create learning environments that support relationships in group care.
Evaluate the parent-provider partnership as a key to understanding children and keeping them connected to the family and culture.

rows.title: Infant Toddler Development and Relationship-based Care
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of biological and environmental factors that influence pre-conception and prenatal health and development.
Differentiate and describe a child's behavior with an understanding of social-emotional development and possible underlying causes of that behavior.
Connect observed behaviors of children, birth to 36 months, to developmental concepts and theories in the physical, cognitive, language, social, and emotional domains.
Plan activities and create learning environments that support relationships in group care.
Analyze the multiple contextual influences on infant and toddler development, including diverse family practices and environments.
Evaluate the parent-provider partnership as a key to understanding children and keeping them connected to family and culture.

rows.title: Early Childhood Administration II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the professional role and responsibilities of running an early childhood program or center.
Apply developmental theories of childhood health, safety, and nutrition to educational programming.
Analyze the key indicators of quality environments for all children and the issues that impact delivering a high-quality curriculum to all children.
Assess evaluation tools that determine the key elements of quality care and community resources available to children and families.

rows.title: Cultural Diversity in Early Childhood Education
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Investigate the nature of cultural diversity in the United States and its implication for developing early childhood curriculum and teaching young children
Critique theories of multiple impacts on young children's social identity
Analyze various aspects of children's experience as members of families who experience social bias and the role of education in reinforcing or contradicting such experiences

Identify and assess components of anti-bias approaches that effectively address all isms and promote culturally and developmentally appropriate interactions that allow for optimal learning and development
Evaluate the impact of personal experiences and social identity on teaching effectiveness

rows.title: Understanding Children with Challenging Behaviors
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify possible factors contributing to challenging behaviors in young children.
Identify strategies for preventing and responding to challenging behaviors, including self-care and stress management strategies.
Explain how sensory processing and brain development can affect young children’s behaviors.
Describe the influence and importance of trusting and nurturing relationships between caregivers and children and between caregivers and families.

rows.title: Sensory Motor Development and Activities
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the principles of sensory motor development
Explain the importance of sensory motor functioning with regard to children's physical, cognitive and social-emotional development.
Identify the correlation of brain development to children's learning and social-emotional development.
Design sensory motor curricula in a developmentally appropriate environment for young children.

rows.title: General College Chemistry
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Solve quantitative and qualitative problems involving matter and energy in chemical and physical changes.
Predict and write chemical equations for common reaction types.
Apply modern models of atomic structure to predict the formation and properties of bonds and molecules.
Relate the physical properties of chemical substances to interparticle interactions and relevant statistical models.
Obtain and analyze experimental data using accepted laboratory procedures and equipment.

rows.title: Chemistry and the Environment
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply scientific inquiry to critically evaluate environmental issues like pollution, ozone depletion, climate change, and acid rain using chemical concepts.
Analyze personal, societal, and global issues in the context of chemistry.
Communicate chemical concepts in the context of global environmental issues such as global warming and air pollution.

rows.title: Organic Chemistry II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and draw structures of organic compounds.
Analyze the physical and spectroscopic characteristics of different functional groups.
Predict the products of chemical reactions involving organic compounds.
Apply chemical reaction mechanisms involving organic moieties to solve multistep synthesis problems.
Interpret the results of spectroscopy to identify the structure of organic compounds.
Employ organic chemistry laboratory techniques and instrumentation in the synthesis, isolation, and identification of organic compounds.

rows.title: Introduction to Chemical Principles
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply a variety of appropriate problem-solving tools, including algebraic manipulation of mathematical formulas, dimensional analysis, and use of mole relationships, to the solution of chemical problems.
Apply fundamental chemical models relating to atomic theory, chemical bonding, solution properties, and gas properties to the analysis and description of chemical systems.
Communicate scientific concepts and data, including the use of standard chemical nomenclature, terminology, and symbolism.
Apply standard laboratory methods to the handling and disposing of chemicals, use of instruments, acquisition and analysis of data, and documentation of procedures and results.

rows.title: Beginning Conversational Cantonese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply correct Cantonese sentence structure at a beginning level.
Conduct a conversation at a beginning level in Cantonese.
Speak and respond at a beginning level in the Cantonese language about Chinese culture.

rows.title: Intermediate Conversational Cantonese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply correct Cantonese sentence structure at an intermediate level.
Conduct a conversation at an intermediate level in Cantonese.
Speak and respond at an intermediate level in the Cantonese language about Chinese culture.

rows.title:
Continuation of Beginning Conversational
Mandarin
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Produce accurate pronunciation and tones of Mandarin at a high beginning level.
Communicate in Mandarin on a variety of familiar situations of everyday life, utilizing practical vocabulary, idiomatic expressions and structures at a high beginning level.
Compare basic aspects of Chinese language and culture using high beginning Mandarin.

rows.title: Beginning Conversational Mandarin for Speakers of Other Chinese Dialects
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally using beginning Mandarin vocabulary and structure.
Identify and produce basic Mandarin sounds and tones in simple conversations.
Analyze and describe elements of Chinese culture using beginning Mandarin.

rows.title: Advanced Conversational Mandarin for Speakers of Other Chinese Dialects
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Speak Mandarin fluently in authentic conversational settings using accurate pronunciation and intonation at an advanced level.
Speak precisely to express sophisticated ideas in authentic, advanced Mandarin and respond to the native style of communication in culturally appropriate ways.
Communicate orally about Chinese culture, using linguistically advanced idiomatic Mandarin.

rows.title: Elementary Chinese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a basic level in Chinese.
Read and/or write in Chinese at basic level.
Explain elements of Chinese culture at a level appropriate for a basic level Chinese language learner.

rows.title: Continuation of Elementary Chinese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a novice mid level in Chinese.
Read and/or write in Chinese at a novice mid level
Explain elements of Chinese culture at a level appropriate for a novice mid level Chinese language level.

rows.title: Intermediate Chinese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a basic intermediate level in Chinese.
Interpret the main ideas and grammatical forms of a written text in Chinese at a basic intermediate level.
Compose short communications in Chinese at a basic intermediate level.
Explain elements of Chinese culture.

rows.title: Continuation of Mid-Intermediate Chinese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a mid-intermediate level in Chinese
Read and write in Chinese at a mid-intermediate level
Explain elements of Chinese culture at a level appropriate for a mid-intermediate level Chinese language learner

rows.title: Continuation of Pre-Advanced Mandarin Chinese for Bilinguals
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a pre-advanced level in Mandarin using correct grammar and pronunciation.
Write coherent, well-constructed essays at a pre-advanced level in Mandarin.
Analyze and summarize authentic cultural and literary texts at a pre-advanced level in Mandarin.

rows.title: Chinese Culture for Heritage Learners
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze important elements of Chinese culture and civilization.
Compare the thoughts and contributions of major Chinese philosophers.
Assess important Chinese technological scientific inventions and achievements from antiquity to 19th century.
Analyze the characteristics of various Chinese literary traditions, the various artistic expressions and their importance in Chinese culture throughout the ages.
Identify customs, traditions, and lives of Chinese people and their influences to Japan and Korea.

rows.title: Intermediate Chinese, Part I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a pre-basic intermediate level in Chinese.
Interpret the main ideas and grammatical forms of a written text in Chinese at a pre-basic intermediate level.
Compose short communications in Chinese at a pre-basic intermediate level.
Explain elements of Chinese culture.

rows.title: Continuation of Intermediate Chinese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally in Chinese at an intermediate level.
Read and write in Chinese at an intermediate level.
Explain elements of Chinese culture at an intermediate level of Chinese.

rows.title: Continuation of Intermediate Chinese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally in Chinese at an intermediate level.
Read and write in Chinese at an intermediate level.
Explain elements of Chinese culture at an intermediate level of Chinese.

rows.title: Introduction to Directing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the critical elements of scenes in professionally-written screenplays and film clips.
Articulate performance styles and techniques to use in directing actors.
Translate scripts into pre-production documents.
Demonstrate the responsibilities of the director at all stages of the filmmaking process.

rows.title: Film/Video Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Perform job responsibilities under the supervision of a film/video industry professional.
Use the knowledge and practical skills gained through the film/video work experience.
Apply work experiences and their relevance and impact on one's educational and/or occupational goals.

rows.title: Introduction to Documentary Film Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain how people in diverse cultures have produced culturally significant documentaries that promote social awareness.
Analyze the social and historical contexts of documentary film in meaningful ways.
Evaluate how the aesthetics and structure of documentary films affect ethics, point of view, and persuasion in visual representation.

rows.title: International Film History (1930s-1960s)
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate motion pictures in the context of world history from the 1930s to the 1960s.
Analyze significant national cinemas, filmmakers, and their contributions to the evolution and diversity of film aesthetics and techniques from the 1930s to the 1960s.
Examine and apply various critical approaches to the study of film from the 1930s to the 1960s.

rows.title: Introduction to Film Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Define the basic vocabulary of film production.
Analyze the aesthetics of filmmaking.
Evaluate how film style establishes the conventions of cinema.
Explore how film technique informs cultural development and social awareness.

rows.title: Films of Alfred Hitchcock
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain how the work of Alfred Hitchcock reflects the evolution of motion picture aesthetics as it relates to traditional art forms.
Apply criteria relative to the examination of the works of an auteur director to Hitchcock.
Analyze the historic and aesthetic significance of the work of Alfred Hitchcock.

rows.title: Cult Cinema
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze cult cinema in relation to a range of film texts.
Evaluate cult films with regard to their form, production, reception and ideologies.
Analyze representations of alternative culture and drug use.

rows.title: Narrative Filmmaking
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Define basic motion picture shooting and editing vocabulary.
Identify and describe rules of continuity in critiquing a short film.
Evaluate the role of editing for dramatic effect in narrative.
Demonstrate command of continuity shooting and editing in making a short film.

rows.title: Cinematography & Lighting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Operate digital video and 16mm film cameras at an intermediate level.
Apply informed lens choices to image making to direct attention and express theme or emotion.
Apply exposure control to create a dramatic scene using multiple lighting and grip tools.
Apply industry practices to work efficiently as a crew member in camera, grip and electric positions.
